title: Calendula
subtitle: The pot marigold: the skin-healing herb of the western apothecary
excerpt: Calendula is the pot marigold, grown in kitchen gardens across Europe for its bright orange-yellow flowers and its long use in skin preparations. It is primarily an external herb: salves, oils, and compresses for wounds, rashes, and dry or inflamed skin. A jar of dried flowers keeps a year in the cupboard.

glossaryTerms.definition: An action that supports wound healing and tissue repair. Vulnerary herbs are traditionally applied externally to cuts, abrasions, and inflamed skin.
An oil in which dried herb has been macerated over heat or in sunlight to extract the herb's active constituents into the oil. The base for salves and balms.

A small-area skin test: apply the preparation to a small patch of inner arm skin and wait 24 hours for any reaction before applying more widely. Recommended for any Asteraceae herb in readers with plant allergies.

content.text: Calendula in the home kitchen is primarily a skin herb: the dried flowers infused into oil, pressed into a salve, or brewed into a compress for dry skin, rashes, minor wounds, and chapped hands. The bright orange pot marigold is one of the most useful and accessible herbs in the western apothecary, grown in almost any garden and harvested through summer. Internal tea use is part of the traditional record but the primary reputation is as a
wound-healing
for the skin. A jar of dried flowers keeps a year in the cupboard.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.
Asteraceae allergy: calendula is a member of the daisy family. Readers with a known allergy to ragweed, chamomile, chrysanthemums, or any other Asteraceae plant should
patch test
any calendula preparation before applying it more widely. Apply a small amount to the inner arm and wait 24 hours. Contact dermatitis from calendula in sensitised readers is documented.
Botanical

Calendula officinalis, family Asteraceae. The pot marigold is an annual (or short-lived perennial in mild winters) with bright yellow-to-orange flowers from late spring to the first frosts. It is distinct from the common French or African marigold (Tagetes species), which has different active compounds and a different safety profile. Parts used are the flower heads, harvested fully open on a dry morning. The petals and the whole flower head are used; the herb is harvested repeatedly through the season as new flowers open. It self-seeds reliably in most gardens.
active compounds and actions

The main active compounds are plant compounds called saponins (linked to calming swelling and helping tissue repair). Flavonoids (antioxidant). And carotenoids (the pigments that give the flower its orange colour and are linked to skin-conditioning properties). The wound-healing action is the primary one: calendula supports tissue repair and reduces inflammation at wound sites and on irritated skin. The antimicrobial action is linked to the resin fraction of the flower head. Together these properties make calendula one of the most useful herbs for external skin preparations.
Traditional uses

Western herbal and folk European traditions have used calendula mainly as a wound herb and a skin herb for centuries. the 17th-century herbalist Nicholas Culpeper described the flowers as useful for inflamed eyes, skin complaints, and fevers. The external applications are the most consistent across the traditional literature: infused oil and salve for minor wounds. Burns, dry skin, chapped skin, nappy rash, and nipple soreness in breastfeeding. The lymphatic action is noted in western herbal practice for swollen glands and chronic inflammatory skin conditions.

Internal use as a tea is traditional but secondary. Calendula tea is used in western herbal practice for gastric inflammation and as a gentle lymphatic and calms swelling herb. It is a mild remedy for internal use, appropriate for a cup of tea rather than a concentrated alcohol extract in most kitchen contexts. The external use remains the main application.
Preparations
The classic preparation is a
infused oil

: dried flowers packed into a jar and covered with olive oil (1 part herb to 5 parts oil by weight), either left to infuse in a warm sunny window for four to six weeks or gently warmed in a double boiler at 60 to 65°C for two to four hours. The oil becomes a deep golden-orange and smells strongly of calendula when it is ready. Strain through muslin and store in a dark glass bottle away from light; keeps for twelve months.

Calendula salve is made from the infused oil: melt 1 part beeswax to 4 parts calendula-infused oil in a double boiler, pour into tins at around 60°C, and leave to set. Apply thinly to dry or irritated skin. A salve in a small tin keeps twelve months in a cool cupboard.

A compress from a strong infusion (one tablespoon of dried flowers per cup. Steeped twenty minutes, cooled to skin-tolerable temperature) is the traditional application for inflamed or sore skin that is not an open wound: apply on clean cloth for ten to twenty minutes.
For internal use, a simple infusion of two teaspoons of dried flowers per cup, steeped covered for ten minutes, is the kitchen preparation. Strain before drinking.
Cautions and cautions

Asteraceae allergy: calendula cross-reacts with other daisy-family plants. If you have a known allergy to ragweed, chamomile, or daisies, patch test any external preparation before wider application. If you react to the patch test, calendula is not the right herb for your skin preparations.
External use is safe for most readers without an Asteraceae allergy. No drug interactions are known for external preparations. Internal use at tea doses is gentle.
